book.title: Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products
book.author: Nir Eyal

confidence_note: Verified in the full text of Hooked. The study shows a correlation, not that the internet causes depression or that email relieves it; Eyal offers the relief explanation as one hypothesis. The old text's first-person user quotes ('I felt bored, I opened Instagram') are not in the book and are dropped.
facts: In 2011, 216 undergraduates at the Missouri University of Science and Technology volunteered to have their internet activity tracked anonymously over the academic year.
At the end, researchers compared the anonymized data with that of students who had visited university health services for symptoms of depression.
Study author Sriram Chellappan wrote that participants with depressive symptoms 'tended to engage in very high email usage', along with more video watching, gaming and chatting.
Eyal: the study showed people with symptoms of depression used the internet more; one hypothesis is that they feel negative emotions more often and turn to technology for relief.
Eyal lists negative emotions such as boredom, loneliness, frustration, confusion and indecisiveness as powerful internal triggers that prompt an almost instant, often mindless action.
His pairings: boredom sends people to dramatic headlines, stress to Pinterest, loneliness to Facebook and Twitter, uncertainty to Google; email answers the question of whether someone needs us.
Once a product is linked to a feeling, users return on their own without external prompts; forming that link can take weeks or months.
scene_details: 216 students' web activity logged anonymously for an academic year
very high email use among students with depressive symptoms
checking email to see if someone needs us
tension: Students with symptoms of depression did not just use the internet more; they checked their email far more, and the reason may be a feeling, not a message.
opening_idea: Start with the 216 students who let researchers log every website they visited for a year.

lessons.idea: Many repeated checks answer a feeling rather than a need for information; noticing which feeling it is gives you a choice.
lessons.anchor: Heavy email checking clustered with depressive symptoms; Eyal reads email as a way to see if someone needs us.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: Someone sees they refresh their inbox mostly on evenings they feel left out, and calls a friend instead.

reflect_final: When you last checked your email or a feed with nothing new expected, what were you feeling just before you did it?

use_cases.situation: A colleague jokes that they check email every five minutes.
use_cases.move: Mention the Missouri study: heavy email checking tracked with low mood. Ask, kindly, whether the checking helps.

use_cases.situation: You open a feed in the evening for the third time.
use_cases.move: Write one word for the feeling on a sticky note before you scroll.

use_cases.situation: A teenager at home spends evenings scrolling.
use_cases.move: Ask what kind of day it was before talking about screen time.

pocket_idea: When you check email with nothing to expect, the inbox may be answering a feeling, not a message.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A Missouri study found that students with depressive symptoms checked their email far more than others.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In 2011, 216 students at a Missouri university let researchers log their internet use for a year. Students who'd sought help for depression used the internet more, especially email, plus video, games and chat. Nir Eyal's reading in Hooked: bad feelings are powerful triggers, and we reach for whatever brought relief last time. It's a correlation, but it explains a lot of checking.
